title: Economic and financial influences

draft.title: Economic and financial influences
card: Growth and recession
In a period of growth, jobs and incomes rise, so people spend more and sales usually rise. In a recession, spending falls and sales usually drop.
Inflation
a general rise in prices over time. A business pays more for wages and materials, and customers can buy less with the same money.
Exchange rate
the value of the Australian dollar against other currencies. A stronger dollar makes imports cheaper but makes Australian exports dearer for overseas buyers.
Interest rates
the cost of borrowing. Higher rates raise a firm's loan repayments and leave customers less to spend, and when banks tighten lending, loans are harder to get.
draft.remember: Economic conditions shape what customers spend. Financial conditions shape what it costs a business to run and grow.

a.q: The Australian economy enters a recession. What is most likely to happen to a furniture retailer in Perth?
opts: Sales fall as customers cut their spending
Sales rise as customers buy more goods
Costs fall because the dollar gets stronger
Sales rise because loans become harder to get
a.why: In a recession, jobs and incomes fall, so people spend less and a retailer's sales usually drop. Rising sales go with growth, not recession.
a.clue: What happens to people's incomes in a recession?

b.q: Liam's winery in the Barossa Valley sells most of its wine to buyers in Japan. The Australian dollar rises against the yen. What is the likely effect?
opts: Its wine costs more in Japan, so sales may fall
Its wine costs less in Japan, so sales may rise
Its imported bottles cost more, so its costs rise
Its loan repayments rise, so its costs go up
b.why: A stronger dollar means Japanese buyers need more yen to pay for the same wine, so it becomes dearer for them and sales may fall. It is tempting to think a stronger dollar helps, but it makes Australian exports dearer and imports cheaper, not dearer. Loan repayments depend on interest rates, not the exchange rate.
b.clue: Think about how many yen a Japanese buyer now needs.

a.best: Sales fall as customers cut their spending

b.best: Its wine costs more in Japan, so sales may fall

problems.detail: The Remember line says economic conditions shape customer spending and financial conditions shape business costs. This contradicts the card. Inflation, an economic condition, raises a business's wage and material costs. Higher interest rates, a financial condition, leave customers less to spend. It could teach students a false split. A better line would be: 'Economic and financial conditions change both what customers spend and what it costs a business to run and grow.'

check.summary: Both questions are sound, with one clear answer each, and the card's facts are correct. The Remember line splits economic influences (spending) from financial influences (costs), which contradicts the card's own inflation and interest-rate points and should be reworded.
